title: Drug-Resistant Superbug Candida Auris Now Confirmed in 23 States as U.S. Cases Surge
excerpt: CDC data show over 3,000 clinical cases in 2026, with 95% of isolates resisting first-line antifungal treatment. Experts say the risk is concentrated in hospitals and nursing homes.
body:
• More than 3,000 clinical cases of Candida auris have been reported across 23 U.S. states in 2026, with Texas, Michigan, and Illinois leading the count.
  • CDC analysis of over 8,000 clinical isolates found 95% were resistant to fluconazole, a frontline antifungal drug, while 15% resisted amphotericin B.
  • Screening cultures doubled from 6,000 to 12,000 between 2022 and 2024, and clinical cases rose from 2,882 in 2022 to 6,197 in 2024.
  • Experts stress the risk is concentrated in healthcare facilities, not the general public, but warn the fungus is difficult to eradicate from hospital environments.

Federal health officials are sounding fresh alarms about the spread of Candida auris, a drug-resistant fungus that has now been confirmed in 23 U.S. states and is proving increasingly difficult to treat with existing antifungal medications. More than 3,000 clinical cases have been reported so far in 2026, according to CDC data, with the fungus continuing its rapid expansion through hospitals and nursing homes.

Texas leads the nation with 706 confirmed cases as of mid-July, followed by Michigan with 503 and Illinois with 366, according to Healthline. The numbers reflect an accelerating trend: annual clinical cases rose from 2,882 in 2022 to 4,428 in 2023 and 6,197 in 2024, according to a CDC report issued in early July.

Resistance Patterns Alarm Researchers

A CDC analysis of 8,033 clinical isolates collected by the Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network during 2022 and 2023 found that over 95% were resistant to fluconazole, a first-line antifungal treatment, with resistance exceeding 90% in every U.S. region except the Midwest. Fifteen percent of isolates were resistant to amphotericin B, and 1% resisted echinocandins — the drug class currently recommended as first-line therapy against Candida auris infections.

Less than 1% of isolates showed resistance to all three major antifungal classes, but the number of pan-resistant cases is rising. The findings were published in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases.

"The rapid emergence around the world and the speed of spread in the U.S. is alarming."

— Susan Huang, MD, University of California Irvine School of Medicine

A Healthcare Crisis, Not a Public One

Experts emphasize that Candida auris poses minimal risk to healthy people in the community. The fungus primarily threatens patients in healthcare settings — particularly those in acute care facilities with chronic illnesses, weakened immune systems, or invasive medical devices such as catheters and breathing tubes.

Researchers have estimated that 30% to 60% of patients who develop Candida auris infections die, though many of those patients had serious underlying conditions. The fungus was first identified in Japan in 2009 and first reported in the United States in 2016. Since then, invasive infections have been documented in 39 states.

"Candida auris is a growing problem among chronically ill persons in nursing homes and hospitals. It is not a problem among the general public," William Schaffner, an infectious disease expert at Vanderbilt University, told Healthline.

Why Hospitals Struggle to Contain It

What makes Candida auris particularly troublesome for healthcare facilities is its environmental persistence. The fungus can survive on surfaces for weeks and is resistant to some common disinfectants. A person can transmit the disease for months after recovering from the illness. In Maricopa County, Arizona, an outbreak spanning April 2022 to February 2023 affected 28 healthcare facilities, according to a study published in Infection Control and Hospital Epidemiology.

"It is often multidrug-resistant, so some antifungals may not be reliable as in other Candida species. It can also persist in healthcare environments, making it difficult to eradicate," Peter Chin-Hong, a professor of medicine at UC San Francisco, told Healthline.

New Research Offers a Glimmer of Hope

Researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison recently identified a promising therapeutic target — a protein called TRK1 that Candida auris requires for skin colonization. The finding, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, could open new avenues for treatment as existing drug options narrow.

"There have been reports of Candida strains developing resistance to that [echinocandin therapy], leading to a very serious infection," said Jeniel Nett, the study's lead researcher, underscoring the urgency of new therapeutic approaches.

Public health experts recommend rigorous hand hygiene when visiting healthcare facilities, screening high-risk patients on admission, and using dedicated disinfection protocols for rooms and equipment. Older laboratory methods can misidentify Candida auris, adding to the challenge of rapid containment.
